rounds.title: ROUND 1 · METAL SLINKY
rounds.question: Does the bottom fall at once?

explain.title: WHY?
lines: The spring holds the bottom up
Letting go sends a wave down

caption: Let go of a hanging Slinky: does the bottom fall right away? 🤯 Metal vs plastic, 1/8 slow motion. What's your guess? 👇 #slinky #physics #science #slowmotion #mythbusting #satisfying
description: We hang a Slinky, let go of the top and watch the bottom. Then we do it again with a plastic Slinky four times lighter, and finally drop both at the same time.

The bottom does not fall at once. The top collapses downwards, but the bottom stays exactly where it was, floating in the air, for about 0.27 s, until the collapsed top reaches it. Then the whole Slinky falls together.

The plastic Slinky (49 g) waits about as long as the metal one (216 g): in the 2012 study by Cross and Wheatland (American Journal of Physics), filmed at 300 frames per second, the collapse time from their model fitted to both Slinkies is 0.27 s.

Why: before the drop, the spring tension holds the bottom up against gravity. Letting go of the top only changes the tension at the top; that change travels down the Slinky and needs about 0.27 s to reach the bottom. Until then, nothing changes for the bottom.
The animation is a simulation built on the measured values of the two Slinkies in that study.
sources_detail: Cross & Wheatland, 'Modeling a falling slinky', Am. J. Phys. 80, 1051 (2012), arXiv:1208.4629. Table 1: slinky A (metal) 215.5 g, 86 turns, collapsed 58 mm, hanging 1.26 m; slinky B (plastic) 48.7 g, 39 turns, collapsed 66 mm, hanging 1.14 m. Filmed with a Casio EX-F1 at 300 frames/s. Table 2: fitted k = 0.69 N/m (A), 0.22 N/m (B); collapse time 0.27 s for both. Observed 10 closed turns at the bottom of A while hanging. Abstract: collapse time typically ~0.3 s for real slinkies.
Masses on screen: 215.5 g shown as 216 g, 48.7 g shown as 49 g; 215.5/48.7 = 4.4, shown as '4x lighter'.

Simulated: each turn is a mass; springs with stiffness N x k and pretension (10 closed turns for A); fully damped contact when turns close (inelastic, as in the paper's model). With these values the simulation hangs 1.25 m (A) and 1.15 m (B) and the bottom starts to move after 0.275 s (A) and 0.277 s (B); the on-screen timer shows the simulation time, truncated to 0.01 s.
